findings.claim: POST https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions. Put the audio in a user message as a content part: {"type":"input_audio","input_audio":{"data":"<base64 of raw file bytes>","format":"wav"}}, next to a {"type":"text","text":"..."} part. The audio must be base64. The docs say URLs are not supported for audio. Accepted format values: wav, mp3, aiff, aac, ogg, flac, m4a, pcm16, pcm24. Support varies by model.

OpenRouter does not publish a byte limit for chat completions. The API reference only lists HTTP 413 'Request payload too large'. For Gemini the upstream limit is 20 MB per request in total (prompt plus inline files). Gemini counts 32 tokens per second of audio (1 min = 1,920 tokens), downsamples input to 16 kbps and mixes it to mono. So a 16 kHz, 16-bit mono WAV (about 32 KB/s raw, about 43 KB/s as base64; 10 s is about 430 KB) is plenty. Higher sample rates only add upload time.

Espressif's esp_audio_codec v2.6.2 supports ESP32-S3. It encodes AAC, OPUS, ADPCM, G711 and others, and decodes MP3, AAC, OPUS, FLAC and others. Encoding the mic stream as AAC (ADTS) and sending format 'aac' (an accepted OpenRouter input format) could shrink uploads several times compared with WAV. The decoder can also play MP3 TTS.

GET /api/v1/models?input_modalities=audio returned 48 entries. Prices are per 1M tokens (input / output / audio-in): google/gemini-3.1-flash-lite (GA, May 2026) $0.25 / $1.50 / $0.50, reasoning optional (effort 'none' allowed, default 'minimal'). google/gemini-3.5-flash-lite $0.30 / $2.50 / $0.30, reasoning mandatory (default 'minimal'). google/gemini-2.5-flash-lite $0.10 / $0.40 / $0.30, but expiration_date is 2026-10-20 (3 days away), so avoid it. mistralai/voxtral-small-24b-2507 $0.10 / $0.30, audio listed as 0.0001 per unit, 32k context. qwen/qwen3.8-omni-flash $0.15 / $0.47 (Alibaba only). xiaomi/mimo-v2.6-flash $0.14 / $0.28, no separate audio price. openai/gpt-audio-mini $0.60 / $2.40, audio in $0.60, audio out $2.40, outputs text+audio. nvidia/nemotron-3-nano-omni-30b-a3b-reasoning:free is free.

Google's pricing page agrees. Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite: input $0.25 (text/image/video) and $0.50 (audio) per 1M, output $1.50. Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite: input $0.30 (including audio), output $2.50. At 32 tokens/s, one minute of speech costs about $0.00096 on 3.1 Flash-Lite and about $0.00058 on 3.5 Flash-Lite. A typical turn (10 s audio, about 300 system tokens, about 150 output tokens) costs roughly $0.0005.

Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite has several provider endpoints. google-ai-studio and vertex/global charge $0.25 / $1.50, audio $0.50. The /flex tiers cost half ($0.125 / $0.75, audio $0.25). The /priority tiers cost $0.45 / $2.70. Vertex eu/us cost $0.275 / $1.65. The ':floor' suffix uses flex endpoints and ':nitro' uses priority endpoints.
Google's model card lists audio and video inputs, MMMLU multilingual 88.9% and an output speed of 363 tokens/s. It names translation as a target use. It contains no Russian-specific ASR benchmark.

The Voxtral Small model card lists its strongest languages as English, Spanish, French, Portuguese, Hindi, German, Dutch and Italian. Russian is not named. Context is 32k (about 30 min for transcription). This makes it a weaker choice for Russian.

OpenRouter now has POST /api/v1/audio/transcriptions (announced May 1, 2026). It accepts JSON {"model":"openai/whisper-large-v3-turbo","input_audio":{"data":"<base64>","format":"wav"},"language":"ru"} or OpenAI-style multipart (file, model). Formats: wav, mp3, flac, m4a, ogg, webm, aac. Multipart is capped at 25 MB and processing at 60 s. The response is {"text":..., "usage":{"seconds","cost",...}}. It is not streamed. Transcription models are listed via GET /api/v1/models?output_modalities=transcription.

26 transcription models are listed. STT is billed per second of audio. openai/whisper-large-v3-turbo costs $0.00000333/s on DeepInfra (about $0.012/h) and $0.0000111/s on Groq ($0.04/h). openai/whisper-large-v3 costs $0.0000075/s, openai/whisper-1 $0.0001/s. openai/gpt-4o-mini-transcribe is token-billed at $1.25 / $5 per 1M. qwen/qwen3-asr-0.6b costs $0.00000333/s.

POST /api/v1/audio/speech takes JSON {model, input, voice, response_format: 'mp3'|'pcm' (default pcm), speed, instructions, provider}. The response is raw audio bytes, not JSON. Content-Type is audio/mpeg or audio/pcm (16-bit little-endian), plus an X-Generation-Id header. Streaming is not required. The docs recommend pcm when latency matters and suggest splitting long text to get the first audio chunk sooner. Most models bill per character. Gemini TTS bills per token.

GET /api/v1/models?output_modalities=speech returned 35 models. Ones that fit Russian: google/gemini-3.8-flash-lite-tts ($0.50 per 1M input-text tokens, $6 per 1M output-audio tokens, 30 voices such as Kore/Puck/Charon). microsoft/mai-voice-2.1-flash ($15 per 1M characters, ru-RU voices Lev, Masha, Grant, Harper). fish-audio/s2.1-pro ($15 per 1M chars; a :free variant exists). hexgrad/kokoro-82m is the cheapest ($0.62 per 1M chars) but has no Russian (8 languages). Voxtral Mini TTS is MP3-only according to the OpenRouter tutorial.

Gemini 3.8 Flash-Lite TTS supports 100+ languages, Russian included. Native output is 24 kHz mono 16-bit PCM. Audio output is 25 tokens per second, so at $6/M it costs about $0.00015 per second of speech (about $0.009/min). Google's page says the price doubles to $12/M on 2027-01-01.

Chat completions can also return audio with "modalities":["text","audio"] and "audio":{"voice":"alloy","format":"wav|mp3|flac|opus|pcm16"}. This needs stream:true. Audio arrives as SSE chunks in choices[].delta.audio.data (base64), with delta.audio.transcript alongside. Only openai/gpt-audio and openai/gpt-audio-mini (plus the Lyria music models) have audio output.
The TTS guide's example model openai/gpt-4o-mini-tts-2025-12-15 returns 404 'Model not found' from GET /api/v1/model/... and does not appear in the speech listing. Do not hardcode it.

Structured outputs work with response_format {"type":"json_schema","json_schema":{"name":...,"strict":true,"schema":{...}}}. Gemini 3.1 and 3.5 Flash-Lite list structured_outputs and response_format among their parameters. Add provider.require_parameters:true so the request only goes to endpoints that honor the schema. One call can therefore return {transcript, reply} or {src_lang, transcript, translation} from audio input.

reasoning {"effort":"none"} or {"enabled":false} turns off thinking. It is rejected on models where reasoning is mandatory (for example gemini-3.5-flash-lite, where 'minimal' is the floor). OpenRouter maps Gemini 3 efforts to thinkingLevel. Provider routing supports sort by latency, preferred_max_latency {p90: ...}, and a 'models' array for automatic fallback. OpenRouter notes extra latency during the first 1-2 min of cold edge caches and when credit balance is low.

The provider object supports order, sort ('price'|'throughput'|'latency'), allow_fallbacks, require_parameters, data_collection:'deny', zdr, only/ignore, and preferred_max_latency/preferred_min_throughput. A top-level "models": ["primary","fallback"] array gives model-level failover. The ':nitro' suffix uses priority endpoints and ':floor' uses the cheapest (flex) ones.

GET /api/v1/models takes input_modalities (text, image, audio, file), output_modalities, supported_parameters, sort (e.g. pricing-low-to-high), q, offset/limit. If output_modalities is omitted, only text-output models are returned. Each entry has id, name, architecture.input_modalities/output_modalities, pricing.{prompt, completion, audio, input_audio_cache, ...} as USD per token (strings), supported_parameters, reasoning.{mandatory, supported_efforts}, supported_voices (TTS) and expiration_date. Tested: ?input_modalities=audio&output_modalities=text&sort=pricing-low-to-high&limit=12 works, returns total_count and links.next, and is about 21 KB per 12 models (the full audio list is about 96 KB). The docs say auth is required, but unauthenticated calls also returned 200 in testing.

The audio-input list also contains: ':batch' variants, which are for the async Batch API (POST /api/v1/batches, 24 h window) and unusable for live voice; router entries (openrouter/auto, openrouter/auto-beta) whose pricing is -1; '~google/gemini-flash-latest' aliases; and models with a non-null expiration_date. Filter all of these out on the device. For a TTS picker use output_modalities=speech and read supported_voices.

Required: 'Authorization: Bearer <OPENROUTER_API_KEY>' and 'Content-Type: application/json'. Optional attribution: 'HTTP-Referer: <app URL>' (needed for rankings), 'X-OpenRouter-Title: <app name>' ('X-Title' is still accepted for backward compatibility), and X-OpenRouter-Categories / X-OpenRouter-App-Visibility: hidden.

Observed with openssl on 2026-10-17: Cloudflare edge, TLS 1.3 (TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384), ECDSA P-256 leaf CN=openrouter.ai valid Oct 17 2026 to Jan 15 2027 (about 90 days, so do not pin the leaf). Chain: leaf <- Google Trust Services 'WE1' <- 'GTS Root R4', with GTS Root R4 cross-signed by 'GlobalSign Root CA'. If you embed PEMs, include both GTS Root R4 and GlobalSign Root CA.

ESP-IDF's x509 certificate bundle (esp_crt_bundle_attach via esp_http_client_config_t/esp_tls_cfg_t .crt_bundle_attach) ships Mozilla NSS roots. There is a full bundle (130+ roots) and a pre-selected 'common' subset (about 38 roots, about 99% market-share coverage). It can be updated through OTA. This is the simplest robust option against certificate rotation.

':free' models are limited to 20 requests/min, plus 50/day if less than 10 credits have ever been purchased or 1000/day with at least 10. GET /api/v1/key returns limit_remaining, usage, is_free_tier and free_model_daily_requests, which is useful for a balance screen in Settings.

Google says access to the 2.5 models is now limited to users who already used them. New projects are pointed to 3.5 Flash-Lite or 3.8 Flash. Current stable Flash-Lite models are gemini-3.5-flash-lite and gemini-3.1-flash-lite.

research:openrouter-ai.recommendation:
Default LLM: google/gemini-3.1-flash-lite. Fallback: google/gemini-3.5-flash-lite, sent together as "models": ["google/gemini-3.1-flash-lite", "google/gemini-3.5-flash-lite"] for automatic failover.

Why this default: 3.1 Flash-Lite is GA, accepts audio, supports structured outputs, and allows reasoning {"effort":"none"} for the lowest latency. It costs $0.25 / $1.50 per 1M tokens and $0.50 per 1M audio tokens, about $0.001 per minute of speech and about $0.0005 per turn. 3.5 Flash-Lite is cheaper on audio ($0.30/M) but always reasons (minimum 'minimal') and costs $2.50/M on output.

Do not use:
- gemini-2.5-flash-lite: it expires 2026-10-20.
- Any ':batch' variant: these are async only.
- Voxtral: Russian is not among its listed languages.
- gpt-audio-mini as the main path: it needs SSE with base64 audio, and its listed audio price looks anomalous.

Pipeline per press:
1. Record 16 kHz, 16-bit mono into PSRAM. Wrap it as WAV, or encode AAC with esp_audio_codec to shrink the upload, then base64 it.
2. POST /api/v1/chat/completions with a text part (system prompt) plus {"type":"input_audio","input_audio":{"data":..., "format":"wav"}}. Also send reasoning {"effort":"none"}, response_format json_schema with strict:true, and provider {"require_parameters":true, "sort":"latency"}.
   - Assistant mode schema: {transcript, reply}.
   - Translator mode schema: {src_lang, transcript, translation}. The prompt gives the two selected languages and tells the model to translate into whichever one was not spoken.
   - Show the transcript and reply in the chat UI.
3. If voice output is on, POST /api/v1/audio/speech with model google/gemini-3.8-flash-lite-tts (supports Russian, about $0.009/min, price doubles 2027-01-01), response_format "pcm" (16-bit LE, 24 kHz mono; read the rate from Content-Type). Feed bytes into I2S as they arrive. TTS fallback: microsoft/mai-voice-2.1-flash with voice ru-RU-Masha or ru-RU-Lev ($15 per 1M chars). For long replies, split TTS by sentence.
4. Optional cheaper STT-only path for a "transcribe" setting: /api/v1/audio/transcriptions with openai/whisper-large-v3-turbo and language "ru" (about $0.012/h). It adds a second round trip, so it is not the default.

Settings picker:
- LLM list: GET /api/v1/models?input_modalities=audio&output_modalities=text&sort=pricing-low-to-high. Drop ids ending in ':batch', the 'openrouter/' routers, anything with negative prices, and anything with a non-null expiration_date. Show name plus pricing.prompt, completion and audio (multiply by 1e6 for $/M).
- TTS list: GET /api/v1/models?output_modalities=speech. Use supported_voices for the voice list.
- Balance: GET /api/v1/key.
- Parse the model JSON (up to about 100 KB) into PSRAM.

Headers: Authorization: Bearer <key> and Content-Type: application/json. Optionally add HTTP-Referer and X-OpenRouter-Title (X-Title is the legacy name).

TLS:
- Use esp_crt_bundle_attach with the full Mozilla bundle. If you embed PEMs instead, include GTS Root R4 and GlobalSign Root CA. Never pin the 90-day leaf certificate.
- Reuse one keep-alive connection for the LLM and TTS calls to avoid a second handshake.
- Keep the key in NVS (ideally encrypted) and enter it with the round-screen keyboard.
open_questions: OpenRouter publishes no byte limit for the chat-completions body; only HTTP 413 is listed. Gemini's upstream inline limit is 20 MB, so short PTT clips are well below any limit, but the exact OpenRouter cap is unconfirmed.

Real time-to-first-token for gemini-3.1-flash-lite with audio input through OpenRouter is unknown. The endpoints API returned latency_last_30m = null. Measure it end-to-end on the device (upload + inference + TTS first byte).

Russian ASR accuracy of Gemini 3.1 and 3.5 Flash-Lite is not benchmarked in the sources; the model card gives only MMMLU 88.9%. A quick A/B test against whisper-large-v3-turbo on Russian clips is advisable.

Does /api/v1/audio/speech with Gemini TTS actually stream progressively (first bytes before synthesis finishes), or does it return the whole buffer at once? The docs say 'raw audio bytestream' and the SDKs support streaming reads, but progressive delivery is unverified.
PCM sample rate per TTS model: 24 kHz mono is documented for MAI-Voice and is Gemini's native rate. Other models may differ, so the firmware should parse the rate/channels parameters in Content-Type.
Voxtral Small's 'audio' price of 0.0001: the unit is unclear (a search snippet says $100 per million seconds, but I could not confirm this on an opened page).
gpt-audio-mini lists audio input and output at $0.60 and $2.40 per 1M, the same as its text prices. That looks inconsistent with gpt-audio ($32/$64), so it may be a listing anomaly.
Whether all providers of xiaomi/mimo-v2.6-flash and qwen/qwen3.8-omni-flash actually accept audio (neither lists a separate audio price) is unverified, as is their Russian quality.
Whether the ESP-IDF 'common' (CMN) bundle subset includes GTS Root R4 / GlobalSign Root CA is unverified. Use the FULL bundle, or test the CMN bundle against openrouter.ai.
GET /api/v1/models answered without Authorization in testing, but the docs say auth is required. Send the key anyway in case this is enforced later.

findings.topic: OpenRouter TTS endpoint (works with only an OpenRouter key)
findings.claim: OpenRouter has an OpenAI-compatible TTS endpoint: POST https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/audio/speech with header Authorization: Bearer <OPENROUTER_KEY>. Body fields: model, input, voice, instructions, speed, response_format. response_format accepts only 'mp3' or 'pcm', and the default is 'pcm'. The response body is raw audio bytes, not JSON: Content-Type audio/pcm (16-bit little-endian) or audio/mpeg, plus an X-Generation-Id header. Errors come back as JSON with status 400/401/402/429/5xx. OpenRouter announced the endpoint on 2026-05-01.

The PCM sample rate depends on the provider. The docs state 24 kHz mono PCM for the Azure MAI-Voice models, and the TTS collection lists 24 kHz/16-bit mono PCM for Gemini TTS. The API reference only says '16-bit little-endian'. Gemini TTS accepts only pcm and returns 400 if mp3 is requested. Voxtral Mini TTS returns only MP3. The firmware should read the rate from the response headers (the tutorial says audio/pcm carries optional rate and channels parameters) and fall back to 24000 Hz.

findings.topic: OpenRouter speech model catalogue and prices (Models API, fetched 2026-10-17)
findings.claim: Per-character prices from GET /api/v1/models?output_modalities=speech: hexgrad/kokoro-82m $0.62/M chars (8 languages, no Russian); fish-audio/drama-3 $2/M UTF-8 bytes (80% promo discount; Cyrillic is 2 bytes per char, so about $4 per 1M Russian chars); heygen/heygen-voice-1-turbo $4/M (50% promo); microsoft/mai-voice-2.1-flash $15/M; x-ai/grok-voice-tts-1.0 $15/M; mistralai/voxtral-mini-tts-2603 $16/M; elevenlabs/eleven-flash-v2.5 and turbo-v2.5 $20/M (50% promo); microsoft/mai-voice-2.1 $22/M; elevenlabs multilingual-v2/v3/v4 $40/M; deepgram/aura-2 $30/M. Token-priced: google/gemini-3.8-flash-lite-tts $0.50/M input + $6/M audio tokens; gemini-3.8-flash-tts $0.50 + $9/M; gemini-3.1-flash-tts-preview $1 + $20/M. Free: fish-audio/s2.1-pro-free:free.

The TTS docs still use openai/gpt-4o-mini-tts-2025-12-15 in an example, but no OpenAI TTS model is listed in the speech Models API today. /api/v1/models/openai/gpt-4o-mini-tts/endpoints and /openai/tts-1/endpoints both return 404. Do not hard-code OpenAI TTS as the OpenRouter default.

Microsoft MAI-Voice-2.1-Flash is served by Azure, costs $15/M chars, and is described as low-latency. It has Russian voices: ru-RU-Grant, ru-RU-Harper, ru-RU-Lev and ru-RU-Masha, each with the ':MAI-Voice-2.1-Flash' suffix. The voice's locale sets the synthesis language, so the translator needs a voice for each target language. It covers 28 locales: cs, da, de, en (AU/GB/IN/US), es (ES/MX), fi, fr, hi, hu, id, it, ko, nb, nl, pl, pt (BR/PT), ro, ru, sv, th, tr, vi, zh-CN. It has no Japanese, Ukrainian or Arabic. Output is mp3 or 24 kHz mono pcm.

findings.topic: Gemini TTS (direct API and via OpenRouter)
findings.claim: Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS supports 130+ languages and Gemini 3.8 Flash-Lite TTS supports 100+. Russian is explicitly listed, and there are 30 prebuilt voices. Called directly (POST https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/interactions), a normal request returns WAV (24 kHz, mono, 16-bit) and stream:true returns headerless raw L16 24 kHz PCM. Pricing: audio is 25 tokens per second. Flash-Lite TTS output costs $6/M tokens until 2026-12-31 and $12/M from 2027-01-01 (Flash: $9, then $18). That is about $0.009 per minute of speech now. My estimate is roughly $10-12 per 1M Russian characters at about 13-15 chars/s. Google AI Studio has a free tier.
Russia and Belarus are not on the list of regions where the Gemini API and Google AI Studio are available.

Endpoint: POST https://api.openai.com/v1/audio/speech. Models: gpt-4o-mini-tts (supports an 'instructions' field for tone/accent/speed), tts-1, tts-1-hd. 13 voices (alloy, ash, ballad, coral, echo, fable, nova, onyx, sage, shimmer, verse, marin, cedar). Formats: mp3 (default), opus, aac, flac, wav, pcm. pcm is 24 kHz 16-bit signed little-endian with no header. Real-time playback is supported through chunked transfer encoding. Russian is in the supported-language list, but the voices are 'optimized for English'. gpt-4o-mini-tts accepts at most 2000 input tokens.

findings.topic: OpenAI TTS/STT pricing and Russia availability
findings.claim: TTS: tts-1 $15/M chars, tts-1-hd $30/M chars, gpt-4o-mini-tts $0.60/M text input tokens + $12/M audio output tokens. STT: whisper-1 $0.006/min, gpt-4o-transcribe $0.006/min, gpt-transcribe $0.0045/min, gpt-4o-mini-transcribe $0.003/min. Russia and Belarus are not on OpenAI's list of supported countries, and using the API from an unsupported country can get the account blocked.

OpenRouter has made no official statement. According to Russian tech media: on 2026-05-11 OpenRouter emailed Russia-linked accounts that it would stop processing their payments ('does not support usage, billing, or payment methods associated with your geography'). Existing credits kept working. Later, accounts with a Russian billing address were cut off from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google models ('All other models remain available'). From about 2026-06-27 there are reports of HTTP 403 'Not available in your region' for requests from Russian IP addresses.

findings.topic: ESP32 playback libraries (MP3 is possible on the S3 if needed)
findings.claim: The ESP32-audioI2S library (schreibfaul1) decodes wav, mp3, aac, flac, opus and vorbis on the ESP32-S3. It has a built-in openai_speech(), which posts stream:true to api.openai.com/v1/audio/speech with the host hard-coded (it would need a patch to point at openrouter.ai). It also has connecttospeech(), which streams Google Translate TTS MP3 over plain HTTP port 80 from translate.google.com.vn. Raw PCM avoids a decoder, but MP3 is a workable fallback.

findings.topic: Unofficial Google Translate TTS (free, no key)
findings.claim: GET https://translate.google.com/translate_tts?ie=UTF-8&tl=<lang>&client=tw-ob&q=<urlencoded>. No auth and no SLA; it returns audio/mpeg (MP3, so a decoder is needed). Tested on 2026-10-17: a 196-character Russian string returned 200 audio/mpeg, and a 210-character string returned HTTP 400. Text must therefore be split into chunks of about 200 characters or less. The gTTS library uses 100-character chunks (GOOGLE_TTS_MAX_CHARS=100).

findings.topic: Microsoft Edge read-aloud TTS (free, unofficial, fragile)
findings.claim: Connects by WebSocket to wss://speech.platform.bing.com/consumer/speech/synthesize/readaloud/edge/v1?TrustedClientToken=6A5AA1D4EAFF4E9FB37E23D68491D6F4 with a time-windowed Sec-MS-GEC token (5-minute windows, so the clock must be accurate). In October 2026 Microsoft made a 'Sec-MS-GEC v2' token mandatory, built from an obfuscated custom SHA-256/CS64 scheme. Old clients got 403 until edge-tts 7.3.0 (2026-10-13). edge-tts requests audio-24khz-48kbitrate-mono-mp3, custom SSML is blocked, and Russian voices include ru-RU-SvetlanaNeural and ru-RU-DmitryNeural. It is free but can break whenever Microsoft changes the token, and it is not an official API.

Auth header: 'Authorization: Api-Key <key>' (service-account key, no folderId needed) or 'Bearer <IAM>'. API v1: POST https://tts.api.cloud.yandex.net/speech/v1/tts:synthesize with URL-encoded fields text (max 5000 chars), lang, voice, speed, and format = lpcm, oggopus (default) or mp3. lpcm is raw PCM with sampleRateHertz 8000, 16000 or 48000, which is ideal for I2S. API v3 (REST https://tts.api.cloud.yandex.net/tts/v3/utteranceSynthesis) offers rawAudio LINEAR16_PCM (default 22050 Hz) or WAV/MP3/OGG_OPUS and returns streamed JSON with base64 audioChunk.data. Synthesis languages are only Russian (about 16+ voices), English, German, Hebrew, Kazakh and Uzbek, which is weak for the translator mode.

Prices including VAT: API v1 synthesis 1,342 RUB per 1M characters (USD list $11.00/M). API v3 0.1626 RUB per request, billed per started 250-character unit, which is about 650 RUB/M if units are full; the livetts model costs 0.25 RUB per unit. Recognition costs 0.1626 RUB per 15 seconds. No free tier is listed.

The free Freemium plan for individuals stopped being sold or renewed on 2026-07-15. Individuals can now buy a package of 1M synthesis characters for 1,000 RUB (valid 1 month) or 1,000 recognition minutes for 1,200 RUB. The REST endpoint is smartspeech.sber.ru/rest/v1/text:synthesize with formats wav16, pcm16 and opus, and the languages are ru, en, kz and ky. The format details come from a search summary of the official page.

POST https://texttospeech.googleapis.com/v1/text:synthesize returns JSON with base64 audioContent, so the firmware must decode base64. Encodings: LINEAR16 (PCM with a WAV header), PCM (headerless 16-bit LE), MULAW, ALAW, MP3 at 32 kbps, OGG_OPUS, M4A. sampleRateHertz is resampled server-side. Pricing per 1M chars: Standard and WaveNet $4 (first 4M chars/month free), Neural2 and Polyglot $16 (1M free), Chirp 3 HD $30 (1M free), Studio $160. Streaming synthesis only works with Chirp 3 HD over gRPC bidirectional streaming, which is not practical on an ESP32.
Google stopped accepting new Google Cloud customers in Russia in March 2022.

POST https://api.elevenlabs.io/v1/text-to-speech/{voice_id}, plus a /stream variant that returns chunked audio. Auth header: xi-api-key. Supports language_code. output_format includes pcm_8000/16000/22050/24000/32000/44100/48000, wav_* at the same rates, ulaw_8000 and alaw_8000. The default is mp3_44100_128, and 44.1 kHz PCM/WAV needs the Pro tier. API pricing: Flash/Turbo $0.04 per 1K chars ($40/M) and Multilingual/v3 $0.08 per 1K ($80/M); the free plan includes 20k Flash characters per month. Through OpenRouter, Flash v2.5 is currently $20/M (promo). ElevenLabs reportedly blocks Russia and Belarus; its help-center page returned 403 to me, so I only have the search snippet.

Supported languages include ru, en, de, fr, es, it, pt, zh, ja, ko, hi, ar, tr, vi and others (20+ with auto-detection). Up to 15,000 characters per request and 5 voices. xAI natively offers MP3, WAV, PCM, mu-law and A-law, but OpenRouter only exposes mp3 and pcm. On OpenRouter it costs $15/M chars.

findings.topic: Fish Audio (cheap or free option on OpenRouter)
findings.claim: Fish Audio S2.1 Pro has a free API until 2026-11-30 under a fair-use policy, with about 90 ms to first audio. It covers 83 languages including Russian, which is a Tier-2 language in the S2 Pro family. On OpenRouter it appears as fish-audio/s2.1-pro-free:free. The free offer is temporary, so it should not be the permanent default.

POST https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/audio/transcriptions with model, input_audio {data: base64, format} or a multipart upload (25 MB cap), plus optional language and json/verbose_json output. research:tts-stt.recommendation:
ARCHITECTURE: Build the 'TTS provider' setting around one main driver, a generic OpenAI-compatible POST {base_url}/audio/speech with a Bearer key, plus 2-3 small special drivers. The device should always ask for raw PCM, stream the chunked HTTPS body into a PSRAM ring buffer, and write it straight to I2S, so no decoder is needed. 24 kHz 16-bit mono is 48 KB/s, so 8 MB of PSRAM holds about 2.5 minutes. Take the sample rate from the Content-Type parameters (default 24000). Split long LLM replies at sentence boundaries (about 150-400 chars) so the first audio arrives sooner and request limits are respected (Google about 200 chars, Yandex 5000, OpenAI 2000 tokens).

DEFAULT (only an OpenRouter key needed): base_url https://openrouter.ai/api/v1, model microsoft/mai-voice-2.1-flash, response_format "pcm" (24 kHz mono), voice ru-RU-Masha:MAI-Voice-2.1-Flash (or Lev, Grant or Harper). It costs $15 per 1M chars, about 1.5 cents per 1000 chars. For the translator, keep a language-to-voice map, because MAI picks the language from the voice's locale; it covers 28 locales. For target languages MAI lacks (ja, uk, ar, ...), or as a cheaper and more expressive choice outside Russia, use google/gemini-3.8-flash-lite-tts with pcm and a voice such as 'Kore'. It covers 100+ languages and costs about $0.009 per minute of audio in 2026; the price doubles on 2027-01-01. Treat fish-audio/s2.1-pro-free:free as a free testing option only, since it ends 2026-11-30. Do not default to OpenAI TTS on OpenRouter; it is not listed right now. The same driver works with OpenAI direct (gpt-4o-mini-tts, pcm 24 kHz, $0.60 + $12 per M tokens; tts-1 $15/M chars) or a self-hosted Piper/Kokoro server by changing only base_url, key and model.

FALLBACK STT (same OpenRouter key): POST /api/v1/audio/transcriptions with a 16 kHz mono 16-bit WAV, model openai/whisper-large-v3-turbo (about $0.012-0.04 per hour) and language='ru' or the translator's source language. openai/gpt-4o-mini-transcribe ($0.003/min) is the higher-accuracy choice. Groq direct (whisper-large-v3-turbo, $0.04/h, 10-second minimum billing) is the fastest alternative.

findings.claim: ESP32-S3-Touch-LCD-1.85 uses an ST77916 LCD (360x360, QSPI: D0-D3 = GPIO46/45/42/41, CLK GPIO40, CS GPIO21, TE GPIO18, backlight GPIO5), CST816 touch (SDA GPIO1, SCL GPIO3, INT GPIO4), a PCM5101 DAC (DIN GPIO47, LRCK GPIO38, BCK GPIO48), an I2S mic (WS GPIO2, SCK GPIO15, SD GPIO39), and a TCA9554PWR IO expander. Touch reset is on EXIO1, LCD reset on EXIO2, TF-card CS on EXIO3. On V2.0/V2.1 the discontinued MSM261S4030H0R mic was replaced by an ICS-43434.

Waveshare ships two demos: an ESP-IDF one (ESP32-S3-Touch-LCD-1.85-Test, needs ESP-IDF >=5.3.1) and an Arduino one (LVGL_Arduino: esp32 core >=3.0.2, LVGL 8.3.10, ESP32-audioI2S 2.0.0, Tools set to 16MB flash and OPI PSRAM). Both come only as a Google Drive zip. Waveshare has no GitHub repo for the plain 1.85; the waveshareteam repos on GitHub are for the 1.85B and 1.85C, which are different boards.

findings.topic: Waveshare demo init details (via community mirror)
findings.claim: A community repo that keeps the Waveshare demo's layout (main/LCD_Driver/ST77916.c, Touch_Driver/CST816.c, EXIO/TCA9554PWR.c, Audio_Driver/PCM5101.c, MIC_Driver/MIC_Speech.c, LVGL_Driver/LVGL_Driver.c) shows the init sequence. It pulses LCD reset on EXIO2 and opens QSPI on SPI2_HOST at 3 MHz to read register 0x04. If the ID is 00 02 7F 7F it uses a custom vendor init table, otherwise the driver default, and then reopens the bus at 80 MHz. TCA9554 (addr 0x20) is on I2C0 (SDA11/SCL10) and touch (addr 0x15) on I2C1 (SDA1/SCL3); both use the legacy driver/i2c.h. That repo is pinned to IDF 5.5.5 and LVGL 8.3.11, and its partition table is factory-only (no OTA).

Mic: I2S_NUM_1 std Philips, 16 kHz, 32-bit, mono, RIGHT slot (BCLK15/WS2/DIN39), samples shifted >>14 to get 16-bit. Speaker: I2S_NUM_0 std TX (BCLK48/LRCK38/DOUT47, no MCLK), volume done in software by scaling samples. No codec control bus is needed.

The PCM5101 is hardware-controlled (no I2C/SPI), generates its system clock from BCK with an internal PLL (so a 3-wire I2S link is enough, no MCLK), and has 2.1 Vrms line-level outputs meant to feed an amplifier. Plain driver/i2s_std.h TX is therefore enough; esp_codec_dev is optional.

esp_codec_dev 1.6.2 supports ES8311/ES8388/ES7210 and similar codecs. It also offers a dummy codec for designs with no codec chip and software volume (audio_codec_new_sw_vol), so it can wrap a PCM5101 + I2S mic if a unified API is wanted.

findings.topic: Best reference implementation (same board, AI voice assistant)
findings.claim: xiaozhi-esp32 (MIT license, ~31k stars) has a board port at main/boards/waveshare/esp32-s3-touch-lcd-1.85. It uses i2c_master on port 0 with esp_io_expander_tca9554 (pulses expander pins 0|1, i.e. EXIO1/EXIO2, to reset touch and LCD), esp_lcd_st77916 with the same register-0x04 panel-ID detection (3 MHz probe, then 80 MHz), and NoAudioCodecSimplex (separate I2S std mic RIGHT slot at 16 kHz in, speaker at 24 kHz out). It drives GPIO7 (PWR_Control) high as a power latch and reads the power button on GPIO6.

xiaozhi now requires ESP-IDF >=6.0.1, recommends v6.1 and dropped IDF 5.x. Its CI builds in the espressif/idf:release-v6.1 container. Its deps include esp_lcd_st77916 ^2.0.2, esp_lcd_touch_cst816s ^1.1.2, esp_io_expander_tca9554 ~2.0.3, esp_lvgl_port ~2.9.0, lvgl ~9.5.0, esp_codec_dev ~1.6.2 and esp-sr 2.4.7. This shows the whole component set we need builds on IDF 6.1.

xiaozhi's sdkconfig.defaults set CONFIG_BOOTLOADER_APP_ROLLBACK_ENABLE=y, CONFIG_ESPTOOLPY_FLASHSIZE_16MB=y and a custom 16 MB partition table: nvs 0x9000/0x4000, otadata 0xd000/0x2000, phy_init 0xf000/0x1000, ota_0 0x20000/0x3f0000, ota_1 /0x3f0000, assets spiffs 0x800000/8M. Its S3 defaults also set CONFIG_SPIRAM_MODE_OCT=y, SPIRAM_SPEED_80M and MBEDTLS_EXTERNAL_MEM_ALLOC=y.

As of Oct 2026 the current releases are v6.1 (27 Aug 2026), v6.0.3 (2 Sep 2026) and v5.5.6 (16 Oct 2026, bugfix). Releases get 12 months of service (recommended for new projects) plus 18 months of maintenance (critical fixes only). That puts v6.1 in its service period. I could not see v5.5's release year (2025 assumed), so it is probably, but not certainly, already in maintenance.

IDF 6.0 removed the legacy I2S/ADC/RMT/timer drivers. The legacy I2C driver is EOL (removal planned in 7.0), and esp_lcd's I2C panel IO now only accepts driver/i2c_master.h. So the Waveshare demo's touch code (legacy i2c + port number) will not build on 6.x and must be rewritten with i2c_master, as xiaozhi does. IDF 6.0 also moved to MbedTLS 4 / PSA Crypto.

In IDF 6.0, cJSON and esp-mqtt left the core and are now managed components (espressif/cjson, latest 1.7.19~2, and espressif/mqtt). wifi_provisioning became espressif/network_provisioning. esp_http_client, esp_http_server and esp_https_ota remain in IDF; the v6.1 tree still has the advanced_https_ota and captive_portal examples.

EIM is the default and recommended installer for IDF 6.x (the legacy install.ps1/export.ps1 method still exists). Install it with winget (Espressif.EIM, or Espressif.EIM-CLI, both 0.20.0 on winget) or the GitHub release eim-cli-windows-x64.exe (v0.20.1, 16 Oct 2026). Key flags: eim install -i <ver> -t esp32s3 -p <path> -n true -a true (-a installs prerequisites, Windows only). eim install --config eim_config.toml reproduces a saved install. eim run "idf.py build" and eim shell run commands with a version's environment. A desktop IDF_PowerShell shortcut and PowerShell activate/deactivate scripts are created under C:\Espressif\tools.

EIM docs say ESP-IDF supports Python 3.10-3.14 and that 3.14 is fully supported on Windows; IDF 6.x needs at least 3.10. An earlier failure with 3.14 (pydantic-core / PyO3 0.24 refusing 3.14) was fixed on all supported branches in Oct 2025. The installed 3.14 should therefore work, and EIM can install Python itself if needed.

findings.topic: Windows path constraint (critical for this PC)
findings.claim: ESP-IDF docs: the build system does not support spaces in the path to ESP-IDF or to projects. The IDF/tools path must be at most 90 characters and should be ASCII-only unless Windows UTF-8 support is on. The user's working dir C:\Users\<user>\OneDrive\Рабочий стол has both a space and Cyrillic, so put IDF in e.g. C:\esp and the project in e.g. C:\dev\round-assistant, outside OneDrive.

pioarduino stable 55.03.312(-1) (Sep 2026) bundles Arduino core 3.3.12 and framework-espidf v5.5.5; 61.04.00-RC1 is a pre-release. The CLI needs Python 3.10-3.14 and installs via get-platformio.py. Changing sdkconfig from Arduino needs custom_sdkconfig, which triggers 'Hybrid Compile'. That path had linker bugs fixed only in Sep 2026 (#533, #546). The official platformio/platform-espressif32 is stuck on IDF 5.5.0, and users there point to pioarduino.

arduino-esp32 3.3.12 (18 Sep 2026) is built on IDF 5.5; 4.0.0-RC1 targets IDF 6.1. The core has a board entry 'Waveshare ESP32-S3-Touch-LCD-1.85' (16MB, OPI PSRAM, a 'custom' partition scheme, and partitions.csv in the sketch folder is picked up). The precompiled libs already set CONFIG_BOOTLOADER_APP_ROLLBACK_ENABLE=y, and initArduino() automatically marks a PENDING_VERIFY image valid unless verifyRollbackLater() is overridden. Other sdkconfig options are fixed. arduino-cli latest is v1.5.1 (Jun 2026).

Espressif's ESP32_Display_Panel Arduino library supports the ST77916 LCD and CST816S touch and lists ESP32-S3-Touch-LCD-1.85 as a built-in board config. It is the realistic route if the Arduino stack were chosen.

espressif/esp_lcd_st77916 2.0.2 supports SPI, QSPI and MIPI-DSI and requires IDF >=5.4. It provides ST77916_PANEL_BUS_QSPI_CONFIG / ST77916_PANEL_IO_QSPI_CONFIG macros, vendor_config.flags.use_qspi_interface=1, and custom init_cmds through st77916_vendor_config_t. Install with: idf.py add-dependency "espressif/esp_lcd_st77916^2.0.2".

espressif/esp_lcd_touch_cst816s 1.1.2 requires IDF >=5.2 and esp_lcd_touch ^1.2.0; ESP_LCD_TOUCH_IO_I2C_CST816S_CONFIG sets .scl_speed_hz=100000, which the i2c_master path uses. The chip only answers I2C after a touch event and reports a single finger. CONFIG_ESP_LCD_TOUCH_CST816S_DISABLE_READ_ID is available for variants whose ID read fails at init.

esp_lvgl_port 2.9.0 (IDF >=5.2, lvgl >=8,<10, LVGL 9 by default) provides lvgl_port_add_disp() for SPI/QSPI panels with buff_spiram, double_buffer, sw_rotate and trans_size options, plus lvgl_port_add_touch(). LVGL's latest release is 9.6.0 (on the registry as 9.6.0~1).

espressif/esp_io_expander_tca9554 2.0.3 (IDF >=5.2) takes an i2c_master_bus_handle_t: esp_io_expander_new_i2c_tca9554(i2c_handle, ESP_IO_EXPANDER_I2C_TCA9554_ADDRESS_000, &io). Waveshare's EXIO1 and EXIO2 are bits 0 and 1 (its Set_EXIO shifts by Pin-1).

LVGL's built-in Montserrat fonts only include ASCII, a few symbols and the built-in icons, so Russian UI text needs a custom font made with the online converter or lv_font_conv (or built_in_font_gen.py) and stored in flash.

CONFIG_BOOTLOADER_APP_ROLLBACK_ENABLE (off by default) boots a new OTA image in ESP_OTA_IMG_PENDING_VERIFY. The app then calls esp_ota_mark_app_valid_cancel_rollback() after its self-test, or esp_ota_mark_app_invalid_rollback_and_reboot() to go back. A reset or power loss before confirming also rolls back, so the self-test should be fast. Rollback needs an otadata partition plus ota_0 and ota_1. CONFIG_BOOTLOADER_APP_ANTI_ROLLBACK is a separate option and should stay off during development.

App partitions must start on 0x10000 boundaries with sizes in 4 KB multiples. otadata must be exactly 0x2000. Data subtypes include nvs, phy, coredump, fat, spiffs and littlefs (0x83). Use CONFIG_PARTITION_TABLE_CUSTOM with CONFIG_PARTITION_TABLE_CUSTOM_FILENAME; the table sits at 0x8000 by default. A factory partition is optional with two OTA slots.

IDF's otatool.py (components/app_update/otatool.py) can write an image to one slot and switch the boot slot over serial: write_ota_partition --slot 1 --input build/app.bin, then switch_ota_partition --slot 1, and switch_ota_partition --slot 0 to go back; read_ota_partition and erase_otadata also exist. This allows A/B testing and instant rollback during development without OTA.
esptool v5 uses hyphenated commands. Back up the whole factory flash with: esptool -p COMx -b 460800 read-flash 0 ALL backup_16MB.bin. Restore with write-flash 0x0 backup_16MB.bin.

For projects that use only registry or git dependencies, Espressif recommends committing dependencies.lock so every build resolves the same component versions. The file must not be edited by hand. idf_component.yml version specs: '==' exact, '~1.2.3' patch updates only, '^1.2.3' minor updates allowed.

Set esp_http_client_config_t.crt_bundle_attach = esp_crt_bundle_attach with CONFIG_MBEDTLS_CERTIFICATE_BUNDLE (full Mozilla bundle or a common ~42-cert subset; custom certs can be added). For streaming (e.g. SSE from OpenRouter, or chunked TTS audio) use esp_http_client_open(len) -> write -> fetch_headers -> read in a loop. Keep-alive connections are reused when the same handle is kept.

NVS keys are at most 15 characters and strings at most 4000 bytes (enough for API keys and model IDs), grouped into namespaces. nvs_commit() is needed to persist changes. nvs_flash_init() errors ESP_ERR_NVS_NO_FREE_PAGES / NEW_VERSION_FOUND mean erase and re-init. NVS encryption is optional.

IDF's examples/protocols/http_server/captive_portal (present in v6.1 with components/dns_server) runs a SoftAP plus a DNS server that answers every query with the AP IP and redirects HTTP to the portal page. It can also send the DHCP Option 114 captive-portal URL. HTTPS requests are not redirected. This is a good secondary path for pasting a long OpenRouter API key from a phone instead of typing it on the round keyboard.

research:firmware-stack.recommendation:
Use plain ESP-IDF v6.1 (C, CMake, idf.py), installed with the EIM CLI. Use xiaozhi-esp32's MIT-licensed Waveshare 1.85 board port as the bring-up reference rather than Waveshare's demo, which is built on legacy I2C, LVGL 8 and IDF 5.x. Fall back to v5.5.6 only if a needed component turns out not to support 6.x; all the display, touch and LVGL components below also work on IDF 5.4 or newer.

Why ESP-IDF v6.1:
- It is in its service period.
- The full component set (esp_lcd_st77916, esp_lcd_touch_cst816s, esp_io_expander_tca9554, esp_lvgl_port with LVGL 9, esp_codec_dev) is proven on IDF 6.1 for this exact board by xiaozhi's CI.
- It gives full sdkconfig control: OPI PSRAM, rollback, cert bundle and the partition table.

Why not the other two:
- pioarduino: Arduino 3.3.12 sits on IDF 5.5.5, and changing sdkconfig needs Hybrid Compile, which only got linker-bug fixes in Sep 2026.
- arduino-cli: the precompiled libs are fixed. Rollback is enabled and auto-confirmed in them, but you cannot tune PSRAM, TLS or LVGL options.

Windows setup (Python 3.14 is supported):
1. `winget install Espressif.EIM-CLI` (or use the eim-cli-windows-x64.exe release).
2. `eim install -i v6.1 -t esp32s3 -p C:\esp -n true -a true`, then commit the saved eim_config.toml so `eim install --config eim_config.toml` rebuilds the same toolchain.
3. Keep the project at C:\dev\round-assistant. The OneDrive Desktop path has a space and Cyrillic, which ESP-IDF does not support.
4. Build and flash with `eim run "idf.py set-target esp32s3"`, `eim run "idf.py build"`, `eim run "idf.py -p COMx flash monitor"`.

Rollback safety in four layers:
1. Before the first flash, back up the stock firmware: `esptool -p COMx read-flash 0 ALL stock_16MB.bin`.
2. Use git with dependencies.lock committed and managed_components/ and build/ ignored.
3. During development, use A/B slots over USB with otatool.py: `write_ota_partition --slot 1 --input build/app.bin`, then `switch_ota_partition --slot 1`, and `--slot 0` to go back.
4. In the field, use CONFIG_BOOTLOADER_APP_ROLLBACK_ENABLE=y with esp_https_ota. The app calls esp_ota_mark_app_valid_cancel_rollback() only after a fast self-test (display up, touch answers, LVGL loop alive, Wi-Fi or NVS readable).

```

  CMakeLists.txt
  sdkconfig.defaults
  partitions.csv
  eim_config.toml
  dependencies.lock (committed)
  .gitignore (build/, managed_components/, sdkconfig.old)
  components/dns_server/   (copied from the IDF captive_portal example)
  main/
    CMakeLists.txt
    idf_component.yml
    main.c   boot order: nvs_flash_init -> board_init -> settings_load -> ui_start
             -> net_start -> ota_selftest_and_confirm
    board/board_185.c
      GPIO7 power latch high
      I2C0 i2c_master on SDA11/SCL10 -> TCA9554, pulse EXIO1/EXIO2 resets
      SPI2 QSPI ST77916: 3 MHz probe of reg 0x04 -> pick init table -> 80 MHz

      I2C1 i2c_master on SDA1/SCL3 -> CST816S (addr 0x15, INT GPIO4)
      I2S1 RX mic: BCLK15/WS2/DIN39, 16 kHz, 32-bit, right slot
      I2S0 TX speaker: BCLK48/LRCK38/DOUT47, software volume
    ui/  (LVGL 9: chat screen, translator screen, settings, round keyboard,
```

Wi-Fi setup: on-device scan list plus the round keyboard is the main path. The SoftAP captive portal (IDF example, DNS redirect plus DHCP Option 114) is the convenient way to paste a long OpenRouter API key and model ID from a phone.

findings.claim: ESP32-S3-Touch-LCD-1.85: 1.85in 360x360 262K-colour round LCD driven by an ST77916 over QSPI, a CST816 capacitive touch chip on I2C, 512KB internal SRAM, 16MB flash and 8MB PSRAM, plus an onboard PCM5101 audio decoder, power amp and MIC.

LCD QSPI pins: SDA0-3 = GPIO46/45/42/41, SCK = GPIO40, CS = GPIO21, TE = GPIO18, backlight = GPIO5, LCD_RST on TCA9554 EXIO2. Touch: SDA GPIO1, SCL GPIO3, INT GPIO4, RST EXIO1. A TE pin exists, so tear-free sync is possible. The FAQ says the mic changed from MSM261S4030H0R to ICS-43434, with circuit changes.

LVGL docs (latest stable v9.6.0) set buffers with lv_display_set_buffers(disp, buf1, buf2, size_bytes, mode). PARTIAL accepts buffers smaller than the screen (at least 1/10 recommended). DIRECT and FULL need display-sized buffers, and FULL redraws the whole screen on any change. Double buffers let rendering and DMA flushing run in parallel. lv_display_set_flush_wait_cb can wait on a semaphore instead of spinning.

LVGL FAQ, partial mode: 1/10 screen is the minimum and 1/5 is recommended, with two buffers flushed by DMA in the background. For tear-free DIRECT mode with 2 framebuffers: only swap the buffer address in flush_cb and call lv_display_flush_ready() from the VSYNC interrupt. For 360x360 RGB565 that is 25.9KB (1/10) or 51.8KB (1/5) per buffer; a full frame is 259.2KB, which only fits in PSRAM.

findings.topic: Tearing on QSPI panels with internal GRAM
findings.claim: Espressif's method for SPI/QSPI panels with GRAM: start writing each frame on the TE signal and keep write speed at least half the panel's read speed. Enable TE in the controller (TEON) and keep write/read scan directions the same, otherwise the method fails. Reference example: display/lcd/lcd_with_te. Estimate: one 259.2KB frame at 80MHz x4 lines (40MB/s) takes about 6.5ms of pure pixel time, so the bus can keep ahead of a ~60Hz panel scan.

Espressif esp_lvgl_port performance guide: draw buffer size matters most. Below 10% of the screen hurts badly, above 25% adds nothing, and internal-SRAM buffers beat PSRAM. Recommended: CPU 240MHz, flash QIO/120MHz, COMPILER_OPTIMIZATION_PERF, LV_ATTRIBUTE_FAST_MEM_USE_IRAM, LV_DEF_REFR_PERIOD=10 (LVGL9), main task on CPU1. Their benchmark (800x480, internal DMA buffers) went from 17 to 41 avg FPS through these steps; PSRAM variants scored 7-31 FPS.

Seeed's XIAO ESP32-S3 round-display LVGL 9 workshop went from about 9 to about 30 FPS. Steps: 240MHz CPU, 80MHz SPI (described as the S3 SPI limit), -O3/LTO, then PARTIAL mode with 2 large partial buffers in internal SRAM (240x120). That beat full-frame PSRAM buffers (~25 FPS) because writing 115KB to PSRAM costs more than an extra render pass. Plain double-buffering with small tiles initially made it slower.

esp_lvgl_port's CMakeLists compiles its ESP32-S3 SIMD assembly blend routines (lv_color_blend_to_rgb565_esp etc.) only when 9.1.0 <= LVGL < 9.2.0. With LVGL 9.5/9.6 (what xiaozhi uses) that acceleration is off, so don't count on it. Issue #621, asking for 9.3 support, was closed without an adaptation.

esp_lvgl_port supports LVGL 8 and 9. Display config has buffer_size, double_buffer, buff_dma (RGB565 only), buff_spiram, plus a 'PSRAM canvas' mode: full-size buffer in PSRAM with a small DMA-capable trans_size buffer in SRAM. sw_rotate cannot be combined with direct_mode or full_refresh. The LVGL task can sleep until there is an invalidate, an animation or a touch interrupt (LVGL9). Perf monitor needs LV_USE_OBSERVER, LV_USE_SYSMON and LV_USE_PERF_MONITOR.

xiaozhi's SpiLcdDisplay uses buffer_size = width*20 lines (360x20 = 14.4KB, about 5.5% of the screen), double_buffer=false, buff_dma=1, buff_spiram=0, swap_bytes=1, LVGL task priority 1 pinned to core 1. That suits a mostly static chat UI but sits below LVGL's 1/10 minimum, so smooth 30fps animation needs bigger, double buffers.

transform_scale, transform_rotate and skew make LVGL allocate one buffer for the whole transformed area (no chunking). opa_layered, blend_mode and bitmap masks use 'simple layers' rendered in LV_DRAW_LAYER_SIMPLE_BUF_SIZE chunks, and LV_DRAW_LAYER_MAX_MEMORY caps the total. So pulse or scale a large orb by animating its width/height, arc angles or plain opa, not transform_scale.

The LVGL docs warn that large box shadows can be slow or memory-hungry. Linear, radial and conical gradients (lv_grad_radial_init, lv_grad_conical_init) only work with LV_USE_DRAW_SW_COMPLEX_GRADIENTS=1. Use them on small objects only, such as an orb glow.

lv_lottie needs ThorVG (LV_USE_THORVG_INTERNAL, C++), LV_USE_VECTOR_GRAPHIC and an ARGB8888 buffer of w*h*4 bytes (a 200x200 animation is 160KB, so PSRAM). Playback defaults to infinite 60fps and is controlled via lv_lottie_get_anim(). Good for small accent icons; a full-screen Lottie on the S3 software renderer is risky.

lv_anim_t: set_var, set_exec_cb, set_values, set_duration, set_delay, set_path_cb (linear, ease_in, ease_out, ease_in_out, overshoot, bounce, step, or custom), set_reverse_duration (replaces playback), set_repeat_count (LV_ANIM_REPEAT_INFINITE), start/completed/deleted callbacks. lv_anim_timeline_create/add/start/set_progress (0-65535)/set_reverse runs coordinated multi-object state transitions.

lv_screen_load_anim(scr, type, time, delay, auto_del) types: NONE, OVER_*, OUT_*, MOVE_*, FADE_IN, FADE_OUT. All input is disabled during the transition, and auto_del deletes the old screen. Full-screen MOVE animations push a whole frame every step over QSPI, so keep them short (~250ms), or use FADE/OVER, or animate only in-screen elements.

lv_arc has MAIN (track), INDICATOR and KNOB parts, NORMAL/REVERSE/SYMMETRICAL modes, set_bg_angles, set_rotation, set_range/value and set_change_rate. For a display-only ring (mic level, progress) remove the knob style and clear LV_OBJ_FLAG_CLICKABLE. lv_arc_align_obj_to_angle and lv_arc_rotate_obj_to_angle place or rotate widgets along the arc.

lv_scale has ROUND_INNER/ROUND_OUTER modes (default 270-degree range, adjustable rotation), coloured sections, and line or image needles that can bind to subjects. lv_arclabel draws text along an arc (set_angle_start/size, set_radius, set_dir, recolor), which suits rim status text and hints. lv_roller supports LV_ROLLER_MODE_INFINITE wrap-around with an anim_duration snap, good for picking language, model or Wi-Fi.

LVGL example lv_example_scroll_translate: a circular container with clip_corner and scroll_snap_y=center. Its LV_EVENT_SCROLL callback projects each child's offset from centre onto a circle with lv_sqrt, writes translate_x and fades distant items, producing a watch-style curved menu for chat history or settings lists.

LVGL's music demo draws a radial spectrum of 20 bars around a circle. It uses lv_draw_triangle inside an LV_EVENT_DRAW_MAIN_BEGIN handler (with LV_EVENT_REFR_EXT_DRAW_SIZE and COVER_CHECK) and is driven by an lv_anim exec_cb that just calls lv_obj_invalidate. The same pattern fits a mic RMS ring or a TTS 'speaking' ring with 24-32 bars.

LVGL Observer: lv_subject_init_int plus bindings such as lv_obj_bind_flag_if_eq let one integer 'assistant state' subject (idle/listening/thinking/speaking/error) drive visibility and styles of UI parts without manual updates. Subjects must be static, global or heap-allocated.

Google: most Wear OS devices are round, and round screens have 22% less UI space than square ones (pi/4 is about 78.5%). Define top, bottom and side margins in percentages to avoid clipping. BoxInsetLayout places content in the square inscribed in the circle. WearableRecyclerView gives curved lists.

Wear OS recommends 48x48dp touch targets (40x40dp allowed in tight cases); the touch area may extend past the visible element. 1dp is 1/160in, so 48dp is about 7.6mm. If 1.85in is the active diameter (about 194.6px/in, 7.66px/mm), 48dp is about 58px and 40dp about 49px on this panel.

Inscribed square = 360/sqrt(2) = 254.6px, so 52.7px (14.6%) margins for fully boxed text. Usable chord width at vertical offset d from centre is 2*sqrt(180^2 - d^2): d=0 gives 360, 40 gives 351, 60 gives 339, 80 gives 322, 100 gives 299, 120 gives 268, 140 gives 226, 160 gives 165px. Layout rows (keyboard, chat bubbles, buttons) should be sized per row from this, plus about 8-12px rim padding for the bezel.

LVGL's built-in Montserrat fonts (12-48px, 4bpp) contain only ASCII, the degree sign (U+00B0), the bullet (U+2022) and FontAwesome symbols. No Cyrillic, so Russian needs custom-generated fonts. Special built-ins cover only Hebrew/Arabic/Persian and about 1000 CJK glyphs.

lv_font_conv (CLI) and the online converter (lvgl.io/tools/fontconverter) take --font (repeatable, to merge fonts), --size, --bpp 1-8, -r ranges, --symbols, --format lvgl|bin, --no-compress, --lv-font-name. --stride needs LVGL 9.3+. Russian range: 0x20-0x7F,0xB0,0x2022,0x401,0x410-0x44F,0x451 (А-я = U+0410-044F, Ё = U+0401, ё = U+0451; the whole Cyrillic block is U+0400-04FF). To keep icons, merge FontAwesome symbols as the built-ins do.

Measured from LVGL v9.4 built-in Montserrat C files (158 glyphs = ASCII plus about 60 icons, 4bpp, uncompressed): glyph bitmaps are 6.6KB at 16px (~42B/glyph), 13.8KB at 24px (~88B), 22.7KB at 32px (~144B), 49.5KB at 48px (~313B), plus about 8B/glyph descriptors and about 3K kerning values. Adding 66 Russian letters costs roughly +3KB at 16px, +6KB at 24px, +10KB at 32px and +21KB at 48px. A 4-size RU+EN set comes to well under 200KB, negligible against 16MB flash.

LVGL Tiny TTF (stb_truetype) builds fonts at runtime at any size from an embedded TTF or a file (lv_tiny_ttf_create_data/_ex), caches 256 glyphs by default and supports lv_tiny_ttf_set_size. FreeType is the heavier option. This lets one Cyrillic TTF serve every size, at a CPU and RAM cost.

lv_keyboard modes: TEXT_LOWER, TEXT_UPPER, SPECIAL, NUMBER, USER_1-USER_4. lv_keyboard_set_map(kb, mode, map, ctrl_map) replaces a layout using buttonmatrix syntax ("\n" ends a row, "" ends the map). Popovers via lv_keyboard_set_popovers(kb,true) plus the LV_BUTTONMATRIX_CTRL_POPOVER flag; the textarea is linked with lv_keyboard_set_textarea.

In LVGL 9.4 source, the constructor attaches the public lv_keyboard_def_event_cb on VALUE_CHANGED. It handles only the strings "abc", "ABC", "1#", close/keyboard, OK, backspace, arrows and newline; any other key text goes into the textarea via lv_textarea_add_text, so UTF-8 Cyrillic labels work (LVGL ships an Arabic map). An RU/EN toggle therefore means USER_1/USER_2 maps for RU lower/upper plus your own handler: remove def_event_cb, or catch "РУС"/"EN"/shift first and forward the rest.

In lv_buttonmatrix each button gets a relative width of 1-15 in the ctrl map, and rows can hold different button counts. Flags: HIDDEN, NO_REPEAT, DISABLED, CHECKABLE, CHECKED, CLICK_TRIG, POPOVER, RECOLOR, CUSTOM_1/2. Buttons are drawn on the fly at about 8 bytes each, versus 100-150B per button widget. HIDDEN spacer keys can taper rows to the circle's chord width.

Samsung Galaxy Watch (round) offers voice input, handwriting and an on-screen keyboard with a choice of QWERTY or 3x4 (phone-keypad) layouts, with two input languages for quick switching. On round watches, voice-first input with a compact keyboard as fallback is the established pattern.

Research designs for round watches put keys on the rim. C-QWERTY arranges QWERTY keys along the circular edge with tap and swipe-word modes. COMPASS is a rotational ring keyboard with dynamically placed cursors that reported about 10 WPM at first and 12.5 WPM after 90 minutes of practice. WrisText uses arc-shaped key groups. I could only read search abstracts; the full papers were blocked (403) or unreadable.

78/esp-wifi-connect (MIT; the Wi-Fi component xiaozhi uses) starts a SoftAP captive portal at http://192.168.4.1 with DNS hijack and stores up to 10 SSIDs/passwords in NVS. The same approach lets the user type the Wi-Fi password and OpenRouter API key on a phone instead of the round screen.

xiaozhi-esp32 is MIT licensed (Copyright 2025 Shenzhen Xinzhi Future Technology Co., Ltd. and Project Contributors). Code can be reused and modified, including commercially, as long as the copyright and licence notice are kept.

xiaozhi has board folders main/boards/waveshare/esp32-s3-touch-lcd-1.85 (plus -1.85b and -1.85c). Waveshare's AI tutorial lists ESP32-S3-Touch-LCD-1.85 as supported (firmware v2.4.0) and says the touch and non-touch 1.85 boards share one firmware.

The board file brings up the ST77916 on QSPI at 3MHz first and reads register 0x04. If it returns 00 02 7F 7F it uses an alternate 'vendor_specific_init_new' sequence (different panel revisions need different init), then runs at 80MHz. It resets the LCD and touch via TCA9554 and toggles chat with the BOOT button. It never initialises the CST816 touch, so the stock xiaozhi UI on this board is button-driven, not touch.

Audio uses NoAudioCodecSimplex, i.e. raw I2S with no codec chip control. Speaker: BCLK GPIO48, LRCK GPIO38, DOUT GPIO47 (PCM5101, both slots). Mic: SCK GPIO15, WS GPIO2, DIN GPIO39, read from the RIGHT slot. Input is 16kHz and output 24kHz.

The device sends Opus audio (hello: 16kHz, mono, 60ms frames; the server may answer with 24kHz) over WebSocket or MQTT+UDP. The server does ASR, LLM and TTS and returns stt/llm (with an 'emotion' field)/tts (start, stop, sentence_start) messages plus Opus frames. Listen modes are auto, manual and realtime. The default server is xiaozhi.me; self-hosted community servers exist. So xiaozhi does not call OpenRouter directly; that needs a self-hosted bridge or a replaced pipeline.

Current xiaozhi requires ESP-IDF v6.0.1 or later (v6.1 recommended; 5.x no longer supported) and pins lvgl ~9.5.0, esp_lvgl_port ~2.9.0, esp_lcd_st77916 ^2.0.2, esp_codec_dev ~1.6.2 and esp-sr 2.4.7. It offers ESP-SR wake word, AEC full duplex only on capable hardware, and 39 UI languages including ru-RU.

xiaozhi's LCD UI is a rectangular flex-column stack: top status bar, status text, scrollable WeChat-style chat (user bubbles right/green, assistant left/gray, max width 85% of the screen, 20-40 messages kept) and a centred emoji box. It isn't designed for a circle, so reuse its plumbing rather than its layout on a round panel.

fbiego/esp32-c3-mini: MIT, LVGL 9, PlatformIO, native SDL build for UI testing, app framework (watchfaces, notifications, settings, music, games). It targets many round boards, including Viewe Echo Ear 1.85 360x360 and Waveshare S3 1.28/1.43/1.75. The same author contributed the LVGL smartwatch demo (PR #7429, merged Jan 2025, with circular lists, tileview navigation and scroll hints), now in lvgl/lv_demos src/smartwatch.

ZSWatch (Zephyr, 240x240 round, LVGL) is GPL-3.0, so use it only as an architecture reference unless you accept copyleft. andygeiss/esp32-watch (MIT, LVGL 9.4) shares one ui.c between a desktop simulator and ESP-IDF firmware and morphs the clock digits into blinking 'assistant eyes' (400ms morph, 140ms blink): a good model for state animations.

lvgl/lv_port_pc_visual_studio (MIT) is a Windows simulator that keeps the exact LVGL resolution, so a 360x360 round UI with a circular mask can be built and animated on the user's Windows PC before flashing. Use its release/ branches for stable LVGL.

research:round-ui.recommendation:
Build the UI with LVGL 9.5.x through esp_lvgl_port 2.9 and esp_lcd_st77916 2.x, the same versions xiaozhi pins. That lets us copy, with its MIT notice, xiaozhi's ST77916 bring-up for this board: read register 0x04 at 3MHz, choose the init table, then run QSPI at 80MHz with swap_bytes. We add the CST816 touch driver ourselves, because xiaozhi's 1.85 board file never starts touch. Don't adopt xiaozhi's protocol, server or rectangular UI: it needs a xiaozhi or self-hosted server, while we want OpenRouter. Its audio approach (raw I2S simplex: mic on the right slot at 16kHz, PCM5101 at 24kHz) and the esp-wifi-connect captive portal are worth reusing.

Rendering settings:
- PARTIAL mode with two internal-SRAM DMA buffers. Start at 360x40 (about 28.8KB each) and grow toward 1/5 of the screen (360x72, 51.8KB each) if RAM allows next to Wi-Fi, TLS and audio. Put the LVGL heap and image cache in PSRAM.
- CPU 240MHz, COMPILER_OPTIMIZATION_PERF, LV_ATTRIBUTE_FAST_MEM_USE_IRAM, LV_DEF_REFR_PERIOD 16 (or 10).
- Pin the LVGL task to core 1 and keep Wi-Fi and audio on core 0. Turn on SYSMON/PERF_MONITOR while developing.
- Don't count on ESP32-S3 SIMD with LVGL 9.2 or newer.
- Leave direct/full mode alone unless tearing shows during full-screen transitions. If it does, use TE on GPIO18 with FULL mode, or simply avoid full-screen MOVE animations.

Round layout:
- Root screen with radius LV_RADIUS_CIRCLE and clip_corner. Keep everything within about 168px of the centre (12px rim padding).
- Fit text blocks inside the 254px inscribed square, or size each row from the chord width.
- Touch targets of at least 50-58px.
- Navigation: a tileview (swipe) between Assistant, Translator and Settings.
- Settings: curved lists using the scroll_translate pattern, lv_roller in INFINITE mode for languages and models, lv_arc for volume and brightness, lv_arclabel for rim status text.

Animated orb:
- One 'orb' component driven by a single lv_subject: idle, listening, thinking, speaking, error.
- Listening: a ring of 24-32 radial bars drawn in DRAW_MAIN_BEGIN, the same pattern as LVGL's music demo, fed with mic RMS at 20-30Hz.
- Thinking: 2-3 rotating lv_arcs on ease_in_out loops, plus a breathing size animation.
- Speaking: the same bar ring fed by the TTS output level.
- State changes run as lv_anim_timeline transitions of 150-300ms with ease_out or overshoot. Screen changes use FADE or OVER at about 250ms.
- Avoid transform_scale on big objects, large shadows and full-screen Lottie. Keep gradients small, with COMPLEX_GRADIENTS enabled.

Fonts:
- Generate 4bpp fonts with lv_font_conv from an OFL font with Cyrillic (Montserrat, Inter or Noto Sans). Range: 0x20-0x7F, 0xA0-0xFF, 0x401, 0x410-0x44F, 0x451, plus punctuation. Merge in the FontAwesome symbols LVGL uses.
- About 4 sizes (16/20/28/40px), roughly 100-200KB in total.
- Optionally Tiny TTF for one large display size.
- Add extra scripts only for translator target languages that need them.

Keyboard:
- Customise lv_keyboard, which is a buttonmatrix, so we keep popovers and textarea linking.
- Maps: USER_1/USER_2 for RU lower/upper, the stock modes for EN, NUMBER/SPECIAL for symbols. Use our own VALUE_CHANGED handler for the RU/EN/shift keys and forward everything else to lv_keyboard_def_event_cb.
- Fit 4 rows in roughly y=125-330, with HIDDEN spacer keys and width ratios tapering each row to the chord: about 6-7 keys of 46-52px per row, popovers on.
- Russian's 33 letters go on two pages or a 3x11 compressed layout with long-press for ё/ъ.
- The text field sits in the upper band.
- An optional rim 'rotary picker' mode (drag around the ring, release to commit), inspired by C-QWERTY and COMPASS, for one-handed entry.
- Make the phone captive portal the main way to enter the Wi-Fi password and OpenRouter API key, and voice dictation the main way to enter chat text.

Process:
- Build and iterate the UI in the LVGL Windows simulator at 360x360 with a circular mask.
- Keep UI code hardware-independent, with git tags per milestone. Together with dual OTA partitions on the device, this covers the user's rollback requirement.
open_questions: Physical active-area diameter of the panel is not stated on Waveshare's product page; px/mm and dp conversions assume 1.85in is the visible diameter (about 7.66 px/mm).
Which ST77916 init path a rev 2.1 board takes in xiaozhi's register-0x04 check (default vs 'vendor_specific_init_new') must be checked on the actual hardware.
Whether the ST77916 on this board needs partial-flush areas aligned to even coordinates (a rounder via LV_EVENT_INVALIDATE_AREA) is unconfirmed; watch for artefacts during partial refresh.
Whether TE (GPIO18) is actually routed and active with esp_lcd_st77916's default init (TEON) is unverified; no ST77916+TE+LVGL example for this board was found.
Exact CST816 variant (CST816S/T/D), its gesture support and single-touch limits on rev 2.1 were not verified; the xiaozhi board file never initialises touch.
Real achievable FPS at 360x360 in PARTIAL mode with 2 internal buffers on this board is unmeasured; run lv_demo_benchmark with SYSMON early.
How much internal SRAM is left for LVGL draw buffers once Wi-Fi, TLS (HTTPS to OpenRouter), I2S DMA and Opus/MP3 decoding run; mbedTLS in PSRAM may be needed.
Whether the flash on this ESP32-S3R8 module supports QIO at 120MHz (one of Espressif's performance steps) is unverified.
Full texts of C-QWERTY, COMPASS and WrisText were not accessible (403 or unreadable PDF); their WPM/error figures come from search abstracts only.
Which translator target languages beyond RU/EN must render on screen (CJK, Arabic, etc.) drives the font budget and needs to be decided.
Whether xiaozhi's RIGHT-slot mic setting still matches the replacement ICS-43434 mic on rev 2.1 needs a hardware check.

verify:openrouter-ai.recommendation_critique:
The overall design holds up: one chat-completions call with audio input and a JSON schema, then a separate /audio/speech call. gemini-3.1-flash-lite is a reasonable default, since it is about $0.00046 per typical turn against about $0.00056 for 3.5-flash-lite. The live data supports both choices. Five things need fixing, and four smaller points are worth adding.

Fixes:

1. The fallback setup is broken. Sending reasoning effort 'none' with models:[3.1, 3.5] means any failover to 3.5-flash-lite (mandatory reasoning) is rejected. Google also says Gemini 3 models cannot turn reasoning off; its 3.1 Flash-Lite mapping only goes down to 'minimal'. So 'none' brings no real latency gain. Send effort 'minimal'. Base the 3.1-vs-3.5 choice on cost per turn, not on 'none'.

2. The pipeline runs everything in series: upload, then wait for the full JSON, then the TTS request, then the first audio. Structured outputs also work with stream:true. Streaming would let the device show text sooner and send TTS sentence by sentence while the reply is still arriving. The SSE parser must:
   - ignore ': OPENROUTER PROCESSING' comment lines;
   - treat a 200 stream containing finish_reason 'error' as a failure.

3. The balance screen is wrong. /api/v1/key returns a per-key cap, which is null when the key has no limit. /api/v1/credits needs a management key, which must not be stored on the device. Set a per-key limit instead. Also warn the user: when the balance is in single-digit dollars, OpenRouter adds extra billing checks and latency goes up.

4. TLS. GlobalSign Root CA is not needed and is no longer in the ESP-IDF v6.x bundles. GTS Root R4 is in the common bundle, so the smaller common (CMN) bundle works.

5. The model picker filter needs three more rules:
   - require supported_parameters to include response_format and structured_outputs. Otherwise the free nemotron and inkling models get no endpoint once require_parameters is set;
   - drop '-preview' duplicates;
   - catch non-'openrouter/' routers such as typesafe/jev-router by their negative price.
   Also check the hardcoded default model ids against /models at boot. Expiry dates are announced only about 3 days ahead: 2.5-flash-lite expires 2026-10-20 and the docs' own example models are already stale.

Smaller points:

- TTS costs more than the LLM. A 10-second Russian reply is about $0.0015 on gemini-3.8-flash-lite-tts. That is roughly three times the LLM call, and it doubles on 2027-01-01 (input and output) on Google's pricing; whether OpenRouter passes the increase on is unknown. Keep the TTS model a setting, with MAI-Voice-2.1-Flash as an alternative. Its voice ids carry the ':MAI-Voice-2.1-Flash' suffix.
- PCM rate parsing: the rate and channels parameters are optional, so default to 24 kHz mono.
- Translator mode: one prompt-based call is fine. The user also wants to choose a provider, though. A configurable OpenAI-compatible base URL would cover both OpenRouter and Gemini direct, since Gemini's compatibility layer accepts input_audio but has no TTS. Google's dedicated gemini-3.5-live-translate-preview (WebSocket Live API, about $0.037/min) is not available on OpenRouter.
- Do not route interactive requests through ':floor' or flex endpoints; the Vertex flex endpoint showed 70% uptime.
missing: The Gemini 3.1 and 3.5 Flash-Lite thinking floor is 'minimal'. Google says reasoning cannot be turned off for Gemini 3 models, so effort 'none' brings no real gain (https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/openai).
Account balance (GET /api/v1/credits) requires a management key. GET /api/v1/key returns only per-key limits, null when the key is unlimited.
Low balance (single-digit dollars) or a key near its credit limit makes OpenRouter add billing checks, which increases latency. This matters for a device with a small prepaid balance.

SSE handling: OpenRouter sends ': OPENROUTER PROCESSING' keep-alive comments, mid-stream errors arrive with finish_reason 'error', and a usage frame comes before [DONE]. Structured outputs can stream partial JSON.
Free audio-input models (nemotron :free, inkling :free, inkling-small :free) do not list response_format or structured_outputs, so they fail when require_parameters:true is set with a JSON schema.
Extra picker entries to filter: typesafe/jev-router (-1 pricing), ~google/gemini-pro-latest, google/gemini-3.1-flash-lite-preview, and xiaomi/mimo-v2.5 (expires 2026-10-21).

Whether /api/v1/audio/speech with google/gemini-3.8-flash-lite-tts accepts response_format 'pcm' and returns the audio progressively is unverified; it needs a test with a real key.

No realtime or WebSocket speech-to-speech models exist on OpenRouter. Google's gemini-3.5-live-translate-preview (Live API, 70+ languages, $0.0053/min in and $0.0315/min out) is an option only through Google directly.

The core choice holds up: plain ESP-IDF v6.1 installed through EIM, with the project at C:\dev, git, a stock flash backup, A/B slots plus bootloader rollback, and xiaozhi as the display/expander/audio reference. Several parts are overstated or wrong.

1. The 'proven on this exact board by xiaozhi CI' argument is weaker than presented. xiaozhi's 1.85 board file never creates a touch device. CI on push/PR builds only changed variants. xiaozhi pins lvgl ~9.5.0, while the recommendation uses ~9.6.0. Touch (CST816T per Waveshare) on IDF 6.1 is therefore unproven and should be the first bring-up milestone. Either pin lvgl ~9.5.0 to match xiaozhi, or accept that 9.6 is untested.

2. The reason given for rewriting Waveshare's I2C code is wrong. Legacy I2C still compiles on 6.x. The real problem is the runtime legacy/new conflict check when it is mixed with i2c_master, which the TCA9554 component needs. The conclusion (use i2c_master everywhere) stands.

3. partitions.csv: the storage line ends with '(fonts, UI sounds)', which is not valid CSV. Comments must be separate lines starting with '#'. The coredump partition does nothing unless CONFIG_ESP_COREDUMP_ENABLE_TO_FLASH is set, and sdkconfig.defaults omits it. The offsets themselves are valid and add up to exactly 16 MB.

4. sdkconfig.defaults leaves out memory settings xiaozhi relies on for TLS + Wi-Fi + LVGL on this board: CONFIG_MBEDTLS_DYNAMIC_BUFFER=y, SPIRAM_MALLOC_RESERVE_INTERNAL=102400 and the reduced Wi-Fi RX buffers. If xiaozhi's LVGL defaults are copied, CONFIG_LV_USE_KEYBOARD=n must be reversed, because the user needs a keyboard.

5. Power: GPIO7 must be driven high first thing in app_main. On battery the board otherwise powers itself off before the rollback self-test can run. Waveshare's wiki confirms only a 'Battery power supply control button' and PWR_Loop(); the GPIO6/GPIO7 numbers come from xiaozhi alone.

6. The speaker path (amplifier part and enable pin) is still unknown. The user said a speaker is not yet connected. The hardware 'speaker volume button' on the board suggests the gain is analog. Keep a text-only mode that works with no audio out.

7. The WU-AetherCore code is PolyForm Noncommercial. Do not copy it; xiaozhi (MIT) is the right reference.

8. The official PlatformIO espressif32 platform does support ESP-IDF 6.1 (v7.1.x). That does not change the choice, but the comparison of alternatives was inaccurate.

9. The skeleton has stt.c and tts.c but no audio decoder or resampler. Whether you need MP3/Opus/WAV decoding (for example espressif/esp_audio_codec) and 16/24/48 kHz conversion depends on the chosen TTS API format. That is a firmware-stack decision left open.

10. Recovery: the board uses native USB-Serial-JTAG (VID 0x303a). If an app breaks USB or boot-loops, the user must enter download mode by hand (hold BOOT, tap RESET). That belongs in the rollback runbook next to the esptool backup.

Disclosure: while checking the winget version I ran `winget show` with --accept-source-agreements, which accepts the winget source terms on this PC. It was read-only otherwise. The amplifier search and the schematic fetch failed (TLS error), and I did not retry the download.
